units.title: Computer Fundamentals
units.overview: What a computer actually is, and the cycle it runs: take data in, process it, put results out, and keep a copy. The chapter sets out the I-P-O cycle, the characteristics that make computers useful, the vocabulary you need to talk about them precisely, and the fields they are used in.
units.summary: A computer follows the I-P-O cycle: input, process, output, with storage alongside. It is fast, accurate, automatic, tireless, versatile and able to hold large amounts of data, and it is used in education, business, medicine, industry, the military, aviation, robotics and design.

detailed.heading: Chapter 1 — Computer Fundamentals
detailed.note: Notes for Chapter 1 of the Class 8 book: the I-P-O cycle, the six characteristics, the vocabulary you need, and where computers are used.
learning_objectives: Describe the I-P-O cycle and give an example of each stage
List the characteristics of a computer and explain what each one means
Use the terms data, information, instruction, program, hardware and software correctly
Give examples of how computers are used in different fields

sections.title: The Working Principle of Computer (I-P-O Cycle)

blocks.text: Every computer, from a pocket calculator to a supercomputer, does the same four things. It takes something in, works on it, hands something back, and keeps a copy. That sequence is called the I-P-O cycle: Input, Process, Output, with storage alongside the whole time.

The word computer comes from the Latin computare, meaning "to calculate". That is a fair description of what the machine does: it is given values and instructions, and it carries out the instructions on the values.
1. Input

Input is the act of giving the computer data and instructions. The devices used to do it are called input devices. Whatever you type, click, scan or speak has to be converted into the electrical signals the machine can work with before anything else can happen.

items: Keyboard — enters text, numbers and commands.
Mouse — a pointing device for moving a cursor and choosing items on screen.
Scanner — turns a paper document or photograph into a digital file.
Microphone — captures sound and converts it into audio data.

blocks.text: 2. Process

Processing is carrying out the instructions on the data — comparing two numbers, adding a column of figures, sorting a list, deciding which branch of a program to follow. It is done by the CPU (Central Processing Unit), the chip that fetches each instruction, works out what it means, and executes it. Processing on its own is useless: it only becomes meaningful once there is data to work on and somewhere for the answer to go.
3. Output
Output is the result handed back to the user after processing. Output devices translate the machine's electrical results back into something a person can read, hear or hold.

items: Monitor — shows visual output on a screen.
Speaker — produces sound.
Printer — puts text or graphics onto paper.
Plotter — prints large graphical output such as maps and engineering drawings.

blocks.text: 4. Storage

Storage holds data and instructions, both while they are being processed and afterwards. Without it, the result of a calculation would vanish the instant it was produced, and the instructions would have to be re-entered every time.
Storage is split into two kinds, and the difference matters:

head: Primary memory
Secondary memory
rows: Hard disk, SSD, pen drive, CD, DVD
Data being worked on right now

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: A common exam slip is to forget storage when drawing the cycle. The cycle is I-P-O, but storage is attached to it — data is read in from storage and results are written back to it. Draw all four.

Boiling a kettle for tea. You put in water, tea leaves and electricity (input). The element heats the water and the tea brews (process). You get a cup of tea (output). The sugar and tea leaves sit in the cupboard until next time (storage).
Six features are what make a computer worth using rather than doing the job by hand. Learn the six names and be able to give a one-line explanation of each.
1. Speed

A computer carries out millions of calculations per second, far beyond what a person can do mentally. Speed is measured in hertz (Hz) — the number of cycles the processor completes each second. Modern machines run at gigahertz, meaning billions of cycles per second.
2. Accuracy

A computer's accuracy is consistently high, close to 100% — but only as good as what it was given. If the data or the instructions are wrong, the answer will be wrong too. This is the principle called GIGO: Garbage In, Garbage Out.
3. Automation

Once you supply the data and the instructions, a computer runs the job by itself. You do not stand over it pressing a button for each step; it carries on until the work is finished or it is told to stop.
4. Diligence

A computer does not get bored, tired or careless. It will repeat the same task thousands of times at the same speed and with the same accuracy, which a person cannot. This is why computers are used for repetitive checking and routine processing.
5. Versatility

The same machine can type a letter, play music, work out a budget and design a building — because its behaviour is decided by the program you load, not by its wiring. Versatility means it can do many different kinds of work in many different areas.
6. Storage capacity
A computer can hold an enormous amount of data and retrieve any part of it quickly. Capacity is measured in these units:

head: Unit
Equals
Notes
rows: Binary digit — the smallest unit of data

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: In computing these units go up in steps of 1024, not 1000, because they follow powers of two. One kilobyte is 1024 bytes. If an exam asks "how many bytes in a kilobyte", the answer is 1024.

sections.title: Some Common Terminologies Related to Computer

blocks.text: Four words are used constantly in computing and are easy to muddle. The distinction between the first pair is the one examiners most like to test.
Raw facts and figures that have not yet been processed — marks, names, temperatures, prices. On their own they do not tell you much.

Data that has been processed, organised and given meaning, so that it is useful for making a decision. A list of every mark in a class is data; the class average and the rank order worked out from it are information.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Data in, information out. Processing is what turns one into the other. If a question asks you to differentiate the two, say this first and then give an example.
A single order telling the computer to do one specific thing — add two numbers, compare two values, move a value into memory.
A set of instructions written in order to carry out a task. A program is what makes the machine versatile: change the program and the same hardware does a different job.
Hardware and software
Together with the four terms above, you need the hardware/software pair:

head: Hardware
Software
rows: The physical parts you can touch
Keyboard, mouse, monitor, CPU, hard disk, pen drive
Operating systems such as Windows and Linux; applications such as MS Word
Wears out and can break physically
Does not wear out, but can have errors ("bugs")

blocks.text: Think of a music player. The player itself, its buttons and its speaker are the hardware. The songs loaded onto it are the software. Neither is much use without the other.

Computers began as huge, expensive machines that only large organisations could afford, and they were used for heavy calculation. Now they are in schools, homes, shops, hospitals and banks, and they are used to learn, work, communicate, keep records and solve problems quickly.
1. Education

Computers serve as a teaching tool as well as a subject. Students research topics online, prepare slides and written work, watch lessons as video, and attend classes over the internet. Educational games and simulations make abstract ideas something you can play with, which keeps learners interested far better than reading alone. Email and online platforms let students and teachers share work and feedback without waiting for a timetabled lesson.
2. Business

Shops use POS (Point of Sale) terminals — the till at the counter. A POS terminal records each sale, prints a receipt listing the items and the total, and updates the stock records automatically, so the shop knows what is left without counting shelves. E-commerce takes the same idea online: products are bought and sold over the internet with electronic payment.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: POS is short for Point of Sale, not "Point of Service" and not "Payment on System". Learn the expansion exactly.
3. Office

Offices prepare letters, reports and documents, and handle accounts, payroll, billing and stock control on computer. When all the work of an office is done this way it is called an electronic office or e-office. The gain is that routine tasks run automatically and the same figures do not have to be typed in twice.

blocks.caption: Use of computers in an office

blocks.text: 4. Communication

Email, video conferencing and social networks all run on computers. They let people speak face to face across continents, or send a message that arrives in seconds instead of the days a letter would take.
5. Banking

Banks record every transaction, keep customer accounts up to date and issue receipts by computer. They provide online banking, electronic transfer of funds and round-the-clock ATM service. Cheques are cleared in large volumes by machines using magnetic-ink character readers (MICR), which read the special characters printed along the bottom of a cheque.

blocks.caption: Use of computers in a bank

blocks.text: 6. Health and medical field

Hospitals keep patient records on computer so that any department can see them, and appointments are booked the same way. Machines such as MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) and CT (Computed Tomography) scanners are computer-controlled and produce detailed images of the inside of the body, which is how doctors diagnose illness without operating. Video links let a doctor consult a specialist in another hospital.

blocks.caption: Use of computers in the health and medical field

blocks.text: 7. Industry

Factories use computers to run machines automatically and to monitor temperature, pressure and other conditions. When something goes wrong the system raises an alarm and isolates the faulty part, which stops a small fault becoming a dangerous one.
8. Military

Modern weapons such as guided missiles, tanks and fighter aircraft are controlled by computer. The targeting system stores detailed maps, compares them with images received in real time and steers the weapon to its target. Unmanned aircraft can be flown into places too dangerous for a pilot.

blocks.caption: Use of computers in the military

blocks.text: 9. Aviation

Airlines keep reservations on computer — flight number, route, distance, seats free and fare — and print tickets on the spot. Passengers see live departure and arrival times. Air traffic control uses computers to manage the landing and take-off of aircraft so that runways are used safely.
10. Robotics

A robot is a machine controlled by a computer program. Robots do repetitive manufacturing work — welding, painting, assembling — faster and more evenly than people, and they can be sent into places unsafe for humans, such as deep mines, areas with radiation, or the seabed.
11. CAD (Computer Aided Design)

Engineers and architects design machines, buildings and electronic circuits on screen using CAD software. It produces precise two-dimensional drawings and three-dimensional models with exact dimensions, and those outputs drive the manufacturing or construction that follows. AutoCAD is a widely used example, in mechanical, civil and electrical engineering alike.

short.question: What is a computer? What is the result obtained after processing data called?
short.answer:
A computer is an electronic device that takes in data and instructions, works on that data following the instructions, gives back the result, and can store data and results for later use. It does all of this at high speed and with consistent accuracy.

The result obtained after processing data is called output. When that output has been arranged so that it actually means something and can be acted on, it is called information.

short.question: What do you mean by automation and diligence of computers?
short.answer:
Automation — once the data and instructions have been given, the computer carries the job through by itself without a person directing each step.

Diligence — the computer can repeat a task any number of times without becoming tired, bored or careless, keeping the same speed and accuracy throughout.

In short: automation is working without being supervised step by step; diligence is keeping it up without wearing out.

short.question: Name any two output devices. Which type of memory stores data temporarily in a computer?
short.answer:
Any two output devices: monitor, speaker, printer, plotter. (For example: monitor and printer.)

The memory that stores data temporarily is primary memory, and the part of it that does this is RAM (Random Access Memory). Everything held in RAM is lost when the power is switched off, which is why work must be saved to secondary storage such as a hard disk or pen drive.

short.question: List two ways computers help students in online learning.
short.answer:
1. Students can attend live classes and watch recorded lessons from home, and can pause or replay them until a difficult point is clear.
  2. Email and online platforms let students send work to a teacher, get corrections back, and discuss questions with classmates without waiting for the next lesson.

Two further ways, if you need them: searching the internet for reference material, and using educational games and simulations to practise an idea interactively.

short.question: Mention two tasks performed by computers in office accounting.
short.answer:
1. Preparing bills and invoices, and keeping the ledger of money received and paid.
  2. Working out payroll — calculating each employee's wages, deductions and the totals — automatically from the hours or salary recorded.

Other acceptable answers: maintaining stock/inventory records, or producing financial reports such as trial balances.

short.question: Name two communication technologies that use computers for real-time interaction.
short.answer:
1. Video conferencing — people in different places see and hear each other at the same moment.
  2. Instant messaging / online chat — typed messages appear on the other person's screen immediately.

Both are real-time because there is no noticeable delay between sending and receiving, unlike email, which waits in an inbox.

short.question: What is online banking and how does it benefit customers?
short.answer:
Online banking is carrying out banking business over the internet instead of visiting a branch — checking a balance, transferring money, paying bills, or opening a deposit.

Benefits to the customer: it is available at any hour, not just during banking hours; it can be used from anywhere with an internet connection; it saves the journey and the queue at the branch; and every transaction is recorded, so the customer can check the history at any time.

short.question: List two computer-assisted diagnostic tools used in hospitals.
short.answer:
1. MRI (Magnetic Resonance Imaging) scanner — produces detailed images of organs and soft tissue using magnetic fields and a computer.
  2. CT (Computed Tomography) scanner — takes a series of X-ray images from different angles and the computer builds cross-sectional views of the body.

Both let a doctor see inside the body without surgery, which is why they are called diagnostic tools.

short.question: How do robots assist in manufacturing processes?
short.answer:
Robots are machines driven by a computer program, so they can be set to repeat one action exactly. In manufacturing they weld, paint, assemble parts and move materials along the line.

They help because they work faster than a person on repetitive jobs, they produce the same result every time, they keep working without a break, and they can be used where fumes, heat or heavy loads would put a worker at risk.

short.question: What is the purpose of AutoCAD software in engineering?
short.answer:
AutoCAD is a CAD (Computer Aided Design) program. Its purpose is to let engineers and architects produce technical drawings on screen — exact two-dimensional drawings and three-dimensional models, with every dimension stated precisely.

Those drawings are then handed to manufacturing or construction, so the part or building is made to the dimensions that were designed. It is used in mechanical, civil and electrical engineering.

long.question: Explain how computers are used as a teaching tool in education.
long.answer:
Computers are used in education both to deliver lessons and to let students produce work of their own.

  • Research. Students search the internet for material on a topic far more quickly than they could find it in a library, and from many sources.
  • Lessons and classes. Teachers present material using slides, pictures and video, which suits learners who take things in visually. Classes can be held online, so a student who is absent or lives far away can still attend.
  • Interactive practice. Educational games and simulations let a student try something and see what happens — change a variable in a circuit or a chemical reaction and watch the result. This keeps attention in a way that reading does not, and it makes abstract ideas concrete.
  • Producing work. Students write assignments, prepare presentations and build spreadsheets, developing the practical skills they will need later.
  • Working with the teacher. Email and online platforms let work be handed in, corrected and discussed without waiting for the next lesson.

The overall effect is that learning becomes faster to arrange, easier to vary for different learners, and more interesting than textbook study alone.

long.question: What is a POS terminal? How does it help businesses?
long.answer:
POS stands for Point of Sale. A POS terminal is the computerised till at the place where the sale is made — the counter in a shop, or the checkout in a supermarket.

What it does: it records each item sold, works out the total, takes the payment, prints a receipt giving the item list and the amount, and updates the stock record so that the quantity left is known immediately.

How it helps a business:

  • Stock is updated as the sale happens, so the owner knows what needs reordering without counting the shelves.
  • The figures are added by machine, so the total is right and the customer is charged the correct amount.
  • The day's sales are recorded automatically, which makes accounts and reporting far easier at the end of the day or month.
  • Service is quicker, so more customers are served in the same time.

long.question: What is an electronic office? How do computers help people communicate?
long.answer:
An electronic office (e-office) is one where the ordinary work of the office is done on computer rather than on paper — letters, reports and documents are written and stored digitally, and accounting, payroll, billing and stock control are handled by software. The result is that routine tasks run automatically and productivity rises.

Communication. Computers give people several ways to reach each other across any distance:

  • Email — a written message sent in seconds rather than the days a letter takes, and it can carry attached files.
  • Video conferencing — people in different places see and hear each other live, which is close to being in the same room and saves the cost of travel.
  • Social media and messaging — quick exchange with individuals or groups, and in the case of messaging, immediate.

Together these make communication faster, cheaper and possible between people who would otherwise never be able to meet.

long.question: How do computers help in banking?
long.answer:
• Recording transactions. Every deposit, withdrawal and transfer is recorded as it happens, so each customer's account is always up to date.
  • Accounts and receipts. Statements and receipts are produced automatically, which removes the errors of hand-written ledgers.
  • Online banking. Customers check balances, transfer funds and pay bills from anywhere, at any hour.
  • ATMs. Cash machines give service round the clock without a cashier.
  • Cheque clearing. Cheques carry characters in magnetic ink that a magnetic-ink character reader (MICR) reads, so thousands of cheques can be processed in the time it would take a clerk to deal with a handful.
  • Security. Records held on computer can be checked and audited, and access controlled by passwords and cards.

long.question: How do computers help doctors and hospitals?
long.answer:
• Patient records. A patient's history, test results and treatment are stored on computer and can be called up by any department that needs them, which avoids repeating tests and losing papers.
  • Diagnosis. MRI and CT scanners are computer-controlled and produce detailed images of the inside of the body, letting a doctor find a problem without operating. Expert systems can also suggest possible causes from the symptoms entered.
  • Appointments. Booking is done on computer, so a hospital can see its schedule and avoid double-booking.
  • Consulting specialists. Video links let a doctor in one hospital discuss a case with a specialist elsewhere, which matters a great deal where the patient cannot be moved.

long.question: How are computers used in the military?
long.answer:
• Guiding weapons. Guided missiles, tanks and fighter aircraft are steered by computer. The system holds detailed maps of the target area, compares them with images arriving in real time, and corrects the course.
  • Unmanned aircraft. Computer-controlled aircraft can fly faster than a pilot could manage and into zones too dangerous for a crew, keeping people out of harm.
  • Planning and simulation. Operations can be rehearsed on computer before they are carried out.
  • Communications. Messages and orders are passed quickly and can be encrypted.

The aim throughout is greater accuracy and less risk to the people involved.

long.question: How do computers help in airlines and airports?
long.answer:
• Reservations. The booking system stores the flight number, route, distance, seats free and fare for every flight, and prints the ticket immediately.
  • Information for passengers. Departure and arrival times and seat availability are shown live on screens and updated as things change.
  • Air traffic control. Computers help controllers manage the landing and take-off of aircraft, so that runways are used safely and aircraft are kept apart.
  • Operation of the aircraft. Modern aircraft themselves rely on computers for navigation and for monitoring engines and systems.

long.question: What work can robots do using computers?
long.answer:
A robot is a machine whose actions are directed by a computer program, so it can repeat an exact movement as often as required.

  • Manufacturing. Welding, painting, assembling parts and moving materials on a production line — done faster and more uniformly than by hand.
  • Dangerous work. Handling radioactive material, working underground, going into fires, or working on the seabed, all places where a person would be at risk.
  • Repetitive or precise work. Anything needing the same action thousands of times, or a movement too fine for the human hand.
  • Exploration and medicine. Reaching places people cannot, and assisting in surgery where steady, tiny movements are needed.

long.question: Explain the applications of computers in any three different fields.
long.answer:
Education. Students and teachers use computers to find information online, prepare lessons and presentations, hold classes over the internet, and practise ideas through educational games and simulations. Work is handed in and returned over online platforms.

Banking. Banks keep accounts, record transactions and issue receipts by computer, provide online banking and ATM service at any hour, and clear large numbers of cheques using magnetic-ink character readers.

Health and medicine. Hospitals store patient records and book appointments on computer; MRI and CT scanners, both computer-controlled, produce images that let a doctor diagnose illness without surgery; and video links allow a specialist in one hospital to advise on a case in another.

(Other fields you could choose: business, office, industry, the military, aviation, robotics, or design with CAD.)

long.question: Write any five areas of use or applications of the computers.
long.answer:
1. Education — research, online classes, presentations, simulations.
  2. Business — point-of-sale terminals, stock records, e-commerce.
  3. Banking — accounts, online banking, ATMs, cheque clearing.
  4. Health and medicine — patient records, MRI and CT scanning.
  5. Industry — running machines automatically, monitoring temperature and pressure.

Other acceptable answers: office (e-office), communication, the military, aviation, robotics, and CAD in engineering.

mcq.question: Which characteristic allows a computer to perform millions of calculations in less than a second?
mcq.teacher_note: Speed is doing a great many calculations in a very short time. Accuracy is about being right, automation about running unaided, versatility about doing different kinds of work.

mcq.question: What does GIGO stand for?
mcq.teacher_note: GIGO is Garbage In Garbage Out: wrong input gives wrong output. Look at the first and last letters — G…O — and the two words are the same in both halves.

mcq.question: Which characteristic enables a computer to work continuously for hours without getting tired?
mcq.teacher_note: Diligence is the ability to repeat work endlessly without tiring or losing care. Speed is how fast, accuracy is how correct, storage capacity is how much can be held.

mcq.question: Which component is responsible for executing data according to instructions?
mcq.teacher_note: The CPU carries out the processing. Input devices supply data, output devices show results, and memory holds data — none of them execute instructions.

mcq.question: Which of the following is an example of an input device?
mcq.teacher_note: A keyboard sends data into the computer. Monitor, printer and speaker all take results out of it, so they are output devices.

mcq.question: How many bytes are in one kilobyte?
mcq.teacher_note: Computing units rise in powers of two, so 1 KB = 2^10 = 1024 bytes. 1000 is the decimal meaning of "kilo" and is the trap answer.

mcq.question: In which field is CAD software commonly used?
mcq.teacher_note: CAD — Computer Aided Design — is for drawing and modelling, so it belongs to design, architecture and engineering.

mcq.question: What does POS stand for in business applications?
mcq.teacher_note: POS is Point of Sale: the place where the sale happens, i.e. the shop counter or till.

mcq.question: Which of the following is NOT a use of computers in education?
mcq.teacher_note: Research, presentations and online classes are all educational uses. Manufacturing cars is an industrial use of computers, not an educational one.

mcq.question: How do computers help students collaborate with teachers?
mcq.teacher_note: Collaboration needs two-way exchange, and email and online platforms give exactly that. Physical letters are slow, and the other two options are nonsense.

mcq.question: What makes learning interactive using computers?
mcq.teacher_note: Interactive means the learner acts and the program responds. Games and simulations do that; writing by hand and physical exercise do not involve the computer responding.

mcq.question: What does a POS terminal process in retail centers?
mcq.teacher_note: A POS terminal is the till: it records each sale. Salaries are a payroll job, and weather and medical records have nothing to do with a shop counter.

mcq.question: What does E-Commerce refer to?
options: Buying and selling products using electronic medium
mcq.teacher_note: E-commerce is commerce done electronically — buying and selling over the internet. Electronic mail is communication, not trade; physical shopping is the opposite of it.

mcq.question: What does a POS terminal print for customers?
options: Receipt with item details and total amount
mcq.teacher_note: The till prints a receipt listing what was bought and the total to pay. The other three are printed by banks, schools and doctors.

mcq.question: What is an electronic office?
options: An office where all work is done using computers
An office with electric lights only
mcq.teacher_note: An e-office is defined by how the work is done — on computer. Staff numbers, lighting and paper are irrelevant to the definition.

mcq.question: Which device do banks use to process cheques?
mcq.teacher_note: Cheques carry characters printed in magnetic ink along the bottom, read by a magnetic-ink character reader (MICR). Typewriters, telephones and radios cannot read a cheque.

mcq.question: What service allows banking transactions using the Internet?
mcq.teacher_note: The question specifies over the internet, and online banking is the name for exactly that.

mcq.question: Which medical imaging device is computer-controlled?
mcq.teacher_note: MRI and CT scanners are built around a computer that builds the image. A stethoscope, thermometer and bandage involve no computer at all.

mcq.question: What do computers control in industry?
mcq.teacher_note: Industrial computers control the process: the machines and the conditions they run under. Menus, parties and holidays are not plant control.

mcq.question: What happens when a fault occurs in a computer-controlled industrial system?
options: The system alarms and disconnects the faulty part
mcq.teacher_note: Control systems are designed to fail safely: raise an alarm and isolate the faulty section. The dramatic answers are not what engineering does.

mcq.question: What do computer-guided missiles use for targeting?
options: Detailed maps stored in computer memory
mcq.teacher_note: Guidance compares stored maps with live images to steer accurately. Guessing, coins and dice are random, which is the opposite of guidance.

mcq.question: What information do computers store for ticket reservations?
options: Flight number, route, distance, seats available, and fare
mcq.teacher_note: A reservation system must hold everything needed to sell a seat: the flight, its route and distance, what is free, and the price.

mcq.question: How do computers help in air traffic control?
options: Controlling landing and takeoff of airplanes
mcq.teacher_note: Air traffic control is about the safe movement of aircraft, so it controls landings and take-offs. Selling tickets is the airline's job, not air traffic control's.

mcq.question: Where can robots be used that are unsafe for humans?
mcq.teacher_note: Robots go where people would be at risk — mines, radiation areas, deep water. Libraries, pools and malls are safe for humans already.

mcq.question: What can CAD software create?
mcq.teacher_note: CAD produces technical drawings and three-dimensional models with exact dimensions. It is not a word processor, music editor or recipe book.

practical.question: Project: IPO cycle demonstration
practical.answer:
Explain the I-P-O cycle in your own words, then show it with a real activity.

  1. Write one paragraph on each stage: what goes in, what the computer does to it, what comes out, and where the data is stored.
  2. Pick a real-life process — making tea, or solving a maths problem — and write down what the input, process, output and storage are for it.
  3. Draw a neat block diagram or flowchart with the four boxes and arrows showing the direction of flow.

practical.question: Project: computers in education
practical.answer:
Describe how you personally use a computer for learning.

  1. List what you do: online classes, learning apps, videos, searching for material.
  2. Explain what each of those does for you — for instance, a video you can pause and replay until a step makes sense.
  3. Give at least three examples of how the computer makes learning easier, faster or more interesting than working from a book alone.

practical.question: Project: computers in communication
practical.answer:
Explain how computers carry messages between people.

  1. Describe three tools: email, video conferencing and social media, and give an example of when each would be the right choice.
  2. Note which of them are immediate (the other person sees it at once) and which wait in an inbox.
  3. Write a short closing paragraph on how these tools make everyday communication quicker and easier than letters or landline calls.

practical.question: Project: hardware vs software collage
practical.answer:
Make a collage contrasting the two halves of a computer system.

  1. Paste or draw pictures of at least four hardware items — mouse, CPU, monitor, pen drive.
  2. List at least three examples of software, such as Windows and MS Word.
  3. Write a short paragraph explaining the difference: hardware is the part you can touch, software is the set of instructions that tells the hardware what to do, and neither is much use without the other.

sections.title: Introduction to Computer Memory and Storage Device

blocks.text:
In everyday life you keep things in your head for the moment and in a notebook for the long term, and you make copies of what matters. A computer does exactly the same, and for the same reasons.

Computer memory is the part of the system that holds data, instructions and results, both while work is being done and afterwards. Everything you do — typing, opening a program, saving a file — involves memory. Without it the machine could not remember anything, so it could do nothing at all.

blocks.title: Two words, one idea
blocks.text: This chapter is about a single question: where does a value live while it is needed now, and where does it live when it must still be there next week? Every device in the chapter answers one of those two.
What memory does

items: Holds the data and the instructions needed for processing.
Holds the intermediate results part-way through a job, and the final result before it is sent to an output device.
Carries all input and output — everything going in or out passes through main memory.

sections.title: Types of Memory — Primary and Secondary

blocks.text: Memory is split by how long it keeps data. Some stores data temporarily, some permanently. That gives the two families:

items: Primary memory (main memory) — works directly with the CPU, fast, mostly temporary.
Secondary storage (auxiliary memory) — holds data permanently, larger, cheaper, slower.

blocks.text: The whole arrangement is usually drawn as a hierarchy. The further down you go, the more you can store, the cheaper each gigabyte becomes, and the longer the processor waits for it.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The trade is always the same: speed against capacity against cost. Fast memory is small and expensive; cheap memory is large and slow. If a question asks why a computer needs both kinds, this is the answer.

Primary memory is the computer's short-term store, also called internal memory. It is connected directly to the CPU, which is what makes it fast, and the computer cannot run without it. Its capacity is limited compared with secondary storage. It comes in three kinds: RAM, ROM and cache memory.
a. RAM (Random Access Memory)

RAM holds the data and instructions of whatever you are running at this moment — your game, your browser, your document — together with the system programs that keep the machine going. Switch the power off and everything in RAM disappears, which is why RAM is called volatile (temporary) memory, and why you are told to save your work.
The more RAM a computer has, the more programs it can run at once without slowing down. RAM comes in two types:

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Static means it holds its value without being refreshed; dynamic means it has to be topped up constantly or the charge leaks away. That single difference explains why SRAM is faster, hotter and dearer.
b. ROM (Read Only Memory)

ROM holds permanent instructions that the computer needs in order to start and operate properly — the startup routines, or firmware/BIOS. Its contents are not lost when the power goes off, so ROM is non-volatile, and they are not meant to be changed in normal use, hence "read only".
There are three kinds, and the difference is how — or whether — you can rewrite them:

head: Type
Full form
How it is changed
rows: Written once; cannot be changed afterwards
Erased with ultraviolet light, then rewritten
Erased and rewritten electrically, without removing it from the computer

blocks.text: c. Cache memory

Cache is a small, very fast, expensive and volatile memory sitting inside or right next to the CPU. It keeps copies of the data and instructions the processor asks for most often, so that the CPU rarely has to wait for the slower main memory. It is built from SRAM, and it acts as a buffer between the processor and RAM.

items: Stores frequently used data and instructions to speed up processing.
Gives the CPU faster access than RAM would.
Acts as a buffer between the CPU and main memory.

blocks.text: Cache inside the CPU is called internal cache; cache outside it is called external cache. Data flows CPU → cache → RAM → hard disk, fastest to slowest.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Exam answers often say "cache is faster than RAM" without saying why. The reason is that it sits nearer the processor and is built from the faster kind of memory, SRAM.

Secondary storage — also called auxiliary memory, external memory or backup memory — keeps programs and data for the future. It is non-volatile, so it holds on to everything when the power is cut, and it is cheaper per gigabyte than primary memory. It exists because RAM is both limited in size and volatile.
The CPU cannot work on data straight from secondary storage. Anything the processor needs is first copied into main memory; results are written back out afterwards.
Features of secondary storage

items: High storage capacity.
Can be used to move data from one computer to another.
Non-volatile — data survives without power.
Cheaper per gigabyte than primary memory, but slower to read and write.

blocks.text: There are four families: magnetic, optical, flash and cloud.
a. Magnetic storage
Magnetic storage is the most common kind of secondary storage. It records data as patterns of magnetisation on a surface coated with iron oxide, on circular discs made of metal or plastic.
i. Hard disk

A hard disk is the main storage device in most computers, and it takes its name from the rigid metal platters inside. It is a direct-access device, meaning any part of the data can be reached without reading through everything before it.

blocks.caption: Showing the upper part and lower part of the hard disk

blocks.text: What a hard disk is for: mass storage of data permanently; long-term holding of the operating system, applications and databases; and large capacity at low cost — at the price of slower reading and writing than RAM or an SSD.
ii. Magnetic tape

Magnetic tape stores data on a thin plastic ribbon, and a tape drive is needed to read and write it. It is a sequential-access device: to reach something in the middle you have to wind past everything before it, which makes it slow for everyday use but fine for archiving.
Tape is used for audio and video, and mainly for backup and recovery — keeping large amounts of data for a long time cheaply, which is why big organisations still use it.
b. Optical disc

An optical disc is a plastic disc read — and sometimes written — using a beam of light. A laser picks up the pattern of pits on the surface. Optical discs are used to distribute software, films and music, to install programs, to back things up, and simply to carry data around.
The common kinds are CD-ROM (Compact Disc Read Only Memory), DVD (Digital Versatile Disc) and Blu-ray Disc (BD).
c. Flash memory
Flash memory is a semiconductor memory with no moving parts. It stores data permanently and is also the easiest way to carry data between machines.
i. Memory chip / card

Memory cards are the standard store for portable devices — phones, tablets, digital cameras, media players and games consoles. They are small, non-volatile, and read and write quickly, and they make it easy to move data from one device to another.
Common formats: SD card, Micro SD, Smart Media Card, Memory Stick, CF (Compact Flash), MMC (Multimedia Card), xD Picture Card, SDHC and Micro SD.
ii. Pen drive

A pen drive is a portable USB flash device, small enough for a pocket and named for being about the size of a pen. It carries audio, video and data files from one computer to another, and it is plug-and-play — no installation needed.
iii. Solid State Drive (SSD)
An SSD stores files, programs and the operating system on electronic memory chips. Unlike a hard disk it has no moving parts — no spinning platter, no read head — which is what makes it fast.
Advantages of an SSD:

items: Very low access time; files transfer much faster.
Uses less power, so laptops and tablets run longer on a battery.
Shock resistant — dropping the device is far less likely to lose data.
Preferred in gaming computers for its short load and write times.

HDD

blocks.text: d. Cloud storage

Cloud storage keeps your files on the internet rather than only on your own disk. It is used for backup, for sharing and for working on the same file with other people, and you need no hardware of your own beyond a connection.

How it works. When you save to the cloud, the file is stored on servers — powerful computers in large data centres — run by companies such as Google, Microsoft or Apple. You reach your files again by signing in from any device: phone, tablet or laptop.
Advantages

items: Files can be reached from anywhere with an internet connection.
No risk of losing files if your own device breaks.
Easy to share with friends and teachers.
Saves space on your own device.
Photos and documents can be backed up automatically.

blocks.text: Disadvantages

items: You need an internet connection to get at your files.
Free storage is limited.
You have limited control, because you depend on the provider.

short.question: What is primary memory?
short.answer:
Primary memory is the computer's main memory, connected directly to the CPU. It holds the data, instructions and results that are being worked on at this moment, and it is what makes fast processing possible.

It is usually volatile — its contents are lost when the power goes off — though ROM is the exception. Examples are RAM, ROM and cache memory.

short.question: List types of ROM.
short.answer:
There are three main types:

  1. PROM (Programmable Read Only Memory) — can be written once only; after that it cannot be changed.
  2. EPROM (Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory) — erased with ultraviolet light and then reprogrammed.
  3. EEPROM (Electrically Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory) — erased and rewritten electrically, without taking it out of the computer.

short.question: Define cache memory.
short.answer:
Cache memory is a small, very fast, expensive and volatile memory placed inside or right next to the CPU. It holds copies of the data and instructions the processor uses most often, so that the CPU rarely has to wait for the slower main memory.

It is made from SRAM, and it acts as a buffer between the processor and RAM.

short.question: Why secondary memory is necessary in a computer?
short.answer:
For two reasons, both about the limits of RAM:

  1. RAM is volatile. Everything in it vanishes at switch-off, so there must be somewhere permanent for the operating system, programs and files.
  2. RAM is limited. It cannot hold the large amounts of data a computer accumulates, so a bigger store is needed.

Secondary storage meets both needs: it is non-volatile, has far greater capacity, and costs less per gigabyte.

short.question: Which flash memory device is commonly used in mobile phones and cameras?
short.answer:
A memory card — a flash memory chip/card such as an SD card or Micro SD card.

It is used in phones, tablets, digital cameras, portable media players and games consoles because it is small, non-volatile, reads and writes quickly, and makes it easy to move data from one device to another.

short.question: Mention any main two advantage of SSD over HDD?
short.answer:
1. Speed. An SSD has very low access time and transfers files much faster, because it has no platter to spin and no head to move.
  2. Durability. With no moving parts it is shock resistant, so dropping the device is far less likely to destroy the data.

A third, if you need one: it uses less power, which lengthens battery life in laptops and tablets.

short.question: Mention any two advantages and disadvantage of cloud storage.
short.answer:
Advantages:

  1. Files can be reached from anywhere, on any device, with an internet connection.
  2. Files are safe if your own device is lost or broken, and can be backed up automatically.

(Others: easy to share with friends and teachers, and it saves space on your own device.)

Disadvantages:

  1. You need an internet connection to get at your files — with no connection, nothing is available.
  2. Free storage is limited, and you depend on the provider, so you have limited control over your own data.

long.question: Write any five differences between RAM and ROM.
long.answer:
BasisRAMROM
1. NatureTemporary (volatile)Permanent (non-volatile)
2. When power goes offData is lostData is kept
3. Read / writeBoth read and writeRead only in normal use
4. What it holdsData and instructions in current useStartup instructions (booting)
5. ChangeabilityEasily read and writtenNot easily changed

long.question: Write two differences between SRAM and DRAM. Explain SRAM.
long.answer:
Two differences:

BasisSRAMDRAM
RefreshingDoes not need to be refreshedMust be refreshed continuously
Speed and costVery fast but expensiveSlower but cheap

SRAM explained. SRAM stands for Static Random Access Memory. It stores each bit using electronic circuits, and because those circuits hold their state on their own, the data does not have to be refreshed again and again — that is the "static" part. The result is a memory that is very fast, but it takes more components per bit, so it is expensive and used only where speed is worth paying for: cache memory.

DRAM ("Dynamic") stores bits as charge in capacitors, which leaks away and has to be topped up constantly. It is slower, but far cheaper, which is why it is used for main memory.

long.question: Define optical discs and mention their uses.
long.answer:
An optical disc is a plastic disc that stores data which is read — and on recordable types written — using a beam of light rather than magnetism. A laser reads the pattern on the surface.

Uses:

  • Distributing films, music and software.
  • Installing programs.
  • Backing up data.
  • Carrying data around — discs are light and portable.

Kinds: CD-ROM, DVD and Blu-ray Disc (BD).

long.question: Explain cache memory and its function in a computer.
long.answer:
Cache memory is a small, special, high-speed, volatile and expensive semiconductor memory placed close to or inside the CPU. It is built from SRAM and holds, temporarily, the data and instructions the processor reaches for most often.

Why it is needed. The CPU is far faster than main memory. Without cache, the processor would spend much of its time waiting for data to arrive from RAM. Cache removes most of that waiting by keeping a copy of the frequently used material right beside the processor.

Its functions:

  1. Stores frequently accessed data and instructions to speed up processing.
  2. Speeds up the CPU's access to data.
  3. Acts as a buffer between the CPU and main memory (RAM).

Cache inside the CPU is internal cache; cache outside it is external cache. Data flows CPU → cache → RAM → hard disk, fastest to slowest.

long.question: You are asked with transferring data from one computer to another. Which type of memory would be suitable for this, and why?
long.answer:
A pen drive (USB flash drive) is the most suitable, and a memory card or an external hard disk would also do the job.

Why a pen drive:

  • It is small and light — it fits in a pocket, so it is genuinely portable.
  • It is plug-and-play: you insert it and it works, with nothing to install.
  • It is non-volatile, so the data survives being unplugged and carried across the building.
  • It is flash memory, so it has no moving parts and survives being knocked about.
  • It works with any computer that has a USB port.

Cloud storage is the other answer worth mentioning: no device to carry at all, but it does need an internet connection at both ends.

long.answer:
Primary memorySecondary storage
1. Holds data and programs currently being executed1. Holds data and programs for future use
2. Directly accessible to the CPU2. Not directly accessible; data passes through primary memory
3. Usually volatile (ROM is the exception)3. Non-volatile
4. Higher cost per bit4. Lower cost per bit
5. Examples: RAM, ROM, cache memory5. Examples: hard disk, CD, DVD, pen drive

long.question: Compare HDD and SSD based on their construction, speed, cost, and advantages.
long.answer:
BasisHDDSSD
ConstructionAluminium circular plates coated with iron oxide; spins a platter and moves a read headSemiconductor NAND flash memory chips; no moving parts at all
SpeedSlower — it must wait for the disc to rotateFaster — low access time, quick read and write
CostLow cost per gigabyteExpensive per gigabyte
AdvantagesCheap for large capacities; well-established technologyFast, low power, shock resistant, quiet

long.question: Why SSD is more popular than hard disk in a modern computer today?
long.answer:
Because the speed difference changes how the whole machine feels, and the other gains matter too:

  1. Speed. With no platter to spin and no head to move, an SSD has very low access time. The computer starts up in seconds and programs open almost at once.
  2. Lower power. It uses less electricity, which lengthens battery life in laptops and tablets.
  3. Durability. Being shock resistant, it is far less likely to lose data when a portable device is dropped — a real advantage in a laptop.
  4. Quiet and cool. No motor means no noise and less heat.

The one remaining drawback is price per gigabyte, and that gap has narrowed steadily, which is why SSDs have become the standard choice.

long.question: Define flash memory and its types.
long.answer:
Flash memory is a semiconductor memory that stores data permanently without needing power. It has no moving parts, and it is equally useful for keeping data and for carrying it from one computer to another.

Types:

  1. Memory chip / card — used in phones, tablets, cameras, media players and games consoles. Formats include SD, Micro SD, Smart Media, Memory Stick, CF (Compact Flash), MMC, xD Picture Card and SDHC.
  2. Pen drive — a portable USB flash device for moving audio, video and data files between computers; plug-and-play.
  3. Solid State Drive (SSD) — flash memory used as the main storage inside a computer, replacing a mechanical hard disk.

long.question: What is cloud storage? Explain how it works.
long.answer:
Cloud storage is a way of keeping files on the internet instead of only on your own computer's hard disk or pen drive. It is used for backup, for sharing, and for several people working on the same file, and it needs no hardware of your own.

How it works:

  1. You save or upload a file, and it travels over the internet.
  2. It is stored on servers — powerful computers in large data centres around the world, owned by companies such as Google, Microsoft or Apple.
  3. To get it back you sign in to your account, and the file comes down to whichever device you are using — phone, tablet or laptop.

Typical free allowances: Google Drive 15 GB, OneDrive 5 GB, iCloud 5 GB, Dropbox 2 GB.

Advantages: access from anywhere, no loss if your device breaks, easy sharing, saves space on your device, automatic backup.

Disadvantages: needs an internet connection, free space is limited, and you depend on the provider.

mcq.question: Which of the following is a primary memory?
mcq.teacher_note: RAM is main memory, directly connected to the CPU. Hard disk, CD-ROM and USB drive are all secondary storage — permanent and slower.

mcq.question: Which memory stores the BIOS firmware?
mcq.teacher_note: ROM holds the startup instructions (BIOS/firmware) and keeps them without power. RAM loses its contents, the hard disk is storage, and cache only holds copies of what is in use.

mcq.question: What is the purpose of cache memory?
options: To provide fast access to frequently used data
mcq.teacher_note: Cache exists purely for speed: it keeps what the CPU asks for most often close at hand. Files are kept permanently by secondary storage, not cache.

mcq.question: Which is the fastest memory in a computer?
mcq.teacher_note: Cache sits nearest the CPU and is built from SRAM, so it beats RAM. Hard disk and CD-ROM are secondary storage and far slower still.

mcq.question: What is the main characteristic of secondary storage?
mcq.teacher_note: Secondary storage is defined by being non-volatile — the data stays after the power goes off. It is slower than RAM, and it is certainly not inside the CPU.

mcq.question: Which storage device uses magnetic disks to store data?
mcq.teacher_note: An HDD records data magnetically on spinning platters. An SSD uses flash chips; CD-ROM and DVD are optical, read with a laser.

mcq.question: What does SSD stand for?
mcq.teacher_note: SSD is Solid State Drive. "Solid state" means the storage is electronic, with no moving parts.

mcq.question: Which storage device has no moving parts?
mcq.teacher_note: An SSD is entirely electronic. The HDD spins a platter, and CD-ROM and floppy drives spin a disc and move a head.

mcq.question: Which is faster: HDD or SSD?
mcq.teacher_note: The SSD wins because it has no platter to spin and no head to move. Colour has nothing to do with it.

mcq.question: Which device uses laser technology to read and write data?
mcq.teacher_note: Optical discs are read with a laser. Hard disks use magnetism; RAM and cache are electronic and use no light at all.

mcq.question: What does USB stand for?
mcq.teacher_note: USB is Universal Serial Bus. "Serial" is the operative word — data goes down the cable one bit after another.

mcq.question: Which storage device is most portable?
mcq.teacher_note: A pen drive fits in a pocket and plugs into any machine. An internal hard disk is fixed in place, and RAM and cache are fitted to the circuit board.

mcq.question: Which memory is used to store data temporarily while the computer is running?
mcq.teacher_note: RAM holds the working data and loses it at switch-off. ROM keeps startup instructions, and secondary storage and CD-ROM are for keeping data, not for the moment.

mcq.question: Which factor is NOT considered when choosing a storage device?
mcq.teacher_note: Capacity, speed and cost are the real criteria — they are the trade-off the whole chapter is built on. Colour affects nothing.

mcq.question: What is the main advantage of HDD over SSD?
mcq.teacher_note: The HDD's one clear win is price per gigabyte. The SSD is faster, tougher and uses less power.

mcq.question: Which memory type is used in digital cameras and smartphones for storage?
mcq.teacher_note: Cameras and phones store photos and files on flash memory cards. RAM and cache are working memory, and ROM holds firmware.

mcq.question: Which storage device is best for backing up large amounts of data?
options: External hard disk or cloud storage
mcq.teacher_note: A backup must be large, permanent and separate from the machine. RAM and cache are volatile and small, and a register holds a handful of bytes.

mcq.question: What is the smallest unit of memory?
mcq.teacher_note: A bit is a single 0 or 1. A byte is 8 bits, and KB and MB are larger still.

mcq.question: How many bits are in three bytes?
mcq.teacher_note: One byte is 8 bits, so 3 × 8 = 24. Watch for 4 (the bits in a nibble) and 16, the usual wrong answers.

mcq.question: Secondary storage is also known as:
mcq.teacher_note: Auxiliary, external and backup memory are all names for secondary storage. Main memory and cache are primary; virtual memory is a different idea altogether.

mcq.question: Which type of memory is a pen drive?
mcq.teacher_note: A pen drive is flash memory — electronic and non-volatile. Magnetic means disk or tape, optical means laser, and cache is processor memory.

mcq.question: Cloud storage stores files on:
mcq.teacher_note: The whole point of cloud storage is that the files sit on servers in a data centre rather than on something you are holding.

mcq.question: Which company provides 15 GB free cloud storage?
mcq.teacher_note: Google Drive gives 15 GB. OneDrive and iCloud give 5 GB, and Dropbox 2 GB.

mcq.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of cloud storage?
mcq.teacher_note: The other three are advantages. Needing a connection is the price you pay for them.

mcq.question: Which memory is cheaper per bit?
mcq.teacher_note: Secondary storage is the cheap, slow end of the hierarchy. Cache and registers are the fastest and by far the dearest per bit.

mcq.question: Data in secondary storage is accessed through:
mcq.teacher_note: The CPU cannot work on data straight from a disk — it is copied into main memory first. Internet and Bluetooth are ways of moving data between machines, not of reading a disk.

teaching_plan.activity: Open with the notebook analogy: what you keep in your head versus what you write down, and why you keep a copy. List the three functions of memory and check them against what happens when you type in a word processor.
Draw the hierarchy on the board, from registers down to cloud. Take RAM and ROM as a five-point comparison, then ask why cache has to exist at all — because the CPU would otherwise wait for RAM.
Compare a hard disk with magnetic tape: direct access against sequential. Pass a CD round and ask how it is read. Place both on the hierarchy drawn last lesson.
Show a pen drive and a memory card. Build the SSD-versus-HDD table: construction, speed, cost, advantages. Ask why an SSD survives being dropped and a hard disk may not.
Ask who already uses Google Drive or iCloud, then trace what happens to a file you upload. Contrast with a pen drive. Finish with unit conversions — bytes to bits, and the 1024 rule.
Work the 26 multiple-choice questions, then the short answers. Set two long answers as homework.

units.title: Number System and Conversion
units.overview: Numbers can be written in different bases. The chapter covers the four systems used in computing — decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal — and how to convert a value between them.
units.summary: Decimal uses ten digits, binary two, octal eight and hexadecimal sixteen. Converting to decimal multiplies each digit by its place value; converting from decimal divides repeatedly and keeps the remainders. Binary and hexadecimal convert via groups of four bits.

detailed.heading: Chapter 3 — Number System and Conversion
detailed.note: Notes for Chapter 3 of the Class 8 book: the four number systems, how to convert between them, and binary arithmetic. Every worked example was checked by executing the conversion.
learning_objectives: Name the four number systems and the digits each uses
Convert a value from any of them into decimal
Convert a decimal value into binary, octal or hexadecimal

blocks.text: You use numbers everywhere — 25 in a maths exercise, a phone number, a price in a shop, a file size in megabytes. But a computer does not hold numbers the way you write them. It stores everything as 0s and 1s, and the same value can be written in several different ways: 25 in decimal is 11001 in binary.
A method of representing numbers using a set of digits or symbols, together with the rules for working out what a written number is worth.

Each system has its own set of digits and its own base (also called the radix) — the number of different digits it has, which is also the value each position is multiplied by as you move left. Four systems are used in computing:

head: System
Base
Digits used
Written as
rows: 0–9 and A, B, C, D, E, F

blocks.text: 1. Decimal number system
The system of everyday life. It uses ten digits, 0 to 9, and each position is a power of 10. It is the base-10 system.
2. Binary number system
The system digital computers and electronic circuits actually use. It has only two digits, 0 and 1, and each position is a power of 2. It is the base-2 system.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: A "binary number" can only contain 0s and 1s. That single rule answers a whole family of questions: if an option contains a 2 or an 8, it cannot be binary.
3. Octal number system
Uses eight digits, 0 to 7, with each position a power of 8 — the base-8 system. The digits 8 and 9 do not exist in it.
4. Hexadecimal number system
Uses sixteen symbols: the digits 0 to 9 and then the letters A to F, where A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14 and F = 15. Each position is a power of 16 — the base-16 system.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Letters stand in for the values 10 to 15 because there are no single digit symbols for them. Learn A–F as 10–15 and the conversions stop being mysterious.
There are only two ideas in this whole section, and which one you use depends on which way you are going.

head: Converting
Method
rows: Multiply each digit by its place value and add
Divide repeatedly by the new base and collect the remainders, reading them bottom to top

blocks.text: Decimal to binary, octal and hexadecimal — divide and collect
The method is the same for all three; only the number you divide by changes (2, 8 or 16).

items: Divide the number by the new base.
Write the quotient underneath — it becomes the new number.
Write the remainder on the right.
Repeat steps 1 to 3 until the quotient reaches 0.
Read the remainders bottom to top — that is the answer.

blocks.text: (47)10 to binary. 47 ÷ 2 = 23 r 1; 23 ÷ 2 = 11 r 1; 11 ÷ 2 = 5 r 1; 5 ÷ 2 = 2 r 1; 2 ÷ 2 = 1 r 0; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Reading the remainders bottom to top gives (101111)2.
(99)10 to octal. 99 ÷ 8 = 12 r 3; 12 ÷ 8 = 1 r 4; 1 ÷ 8 = 0 r 1. Reading bottom to top gives (143)8.
(424)10 to hexadecimal. 424 ÷ 16 = 26 r 8; 26 ÷ 16 = 1 r 10, which is written A; 1 ÷ 16 = 0 r 1. Reading bottom to top gives (1A8)16.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Any remainder of 10 or more must be written as its letter — A for 10, B for 11, C for 12, D for 13, E for 14, F for 15. Forgetting to turn the 10 into an A is the most common mistake in hexadecimal conversion.
Binary, octal and hexadecimal to decimal — multiply and add

items: Number the positions from the right, starting at 0.
Multiply each digit by its base raised to that position.
Add the results together.

blocks.text: (1011)2 to decimal. 1×23 + 0×22 + 1×21 + 1×20 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = (11)10.
(1A8)16 to decimal. A is 10, so 1×162 + 10×161 + 8×160 = 256 + 160 + 8 = (424)10 — which is the number we started from above, so the two methods agree.
(17)8 to decimal. 1×81 + 7×80 = 8 + 7 = (15)10.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Always convert back as a check. If you turn 424 into 1A8 and then 1A8 back into 424, you know both steps are right. It costs ten seconds and catches most slips.

sections.title: Binary Addition, Subtraction, Multiplication and Division

blocks.text: Arithmetic in binary follows the same rules you already use; there are simply fewer digits to combine.
1. Binary addition

items: 1 + 1 = 10 — write 0 and carry 1

blocks.text: 10111 + 11001 = 110000. (Check: 23 + 25 = 48, and 110000 in binary is 48.)
2. Binary subtraction

items: 0 − 1 = 1, borrowing 1 from the next column

blocks.text: 101101 − 10111 = 10110. (Check: 45 − 23 = 22, and 10110 in binary is 22.)
3. Binary multiplication
4. Binary division

items: 1 ÷ 0 is not defined
0 ÷ 0 is not defined

blocks.text: 101011 ÷ 110 gives quotient 111 and remainder 1. (Check: 43 ÷ 6 = 7 remainder 1, and 111 in binary is 7.)

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: A quick way to check any binary arithmetic answer: convert the question and your answer back to decimal and do the sum there. If 10111 + 11001 = 110000, then 23 + 25 must equal 48 — and it does.

short.question: Define the base or radix of a number system.
short.answer:
The base (or radix) of a number system is the number of different digits or symbols it uses. It is also the value by which a position increases as you move one place to the left.

So decimal has base 10, binary base 2, octal base 8 and hexadecimal base 16.

short.question: Convert (77)<sub>8</sub> into a decimal number.
short.answer:
7×81 + 7×80 = 56 + 7 = 63

So (77)8 = (63)10.

short.question: What is binary number system?
short.answer:
The binary number system is the base-2 system. It uses only two digits, 0 and 1, and every position is a power of 2.

It is the system computers use, because a circuit is most reliably built with two states — off and on — which map directly onto 0 and 1.

short.question: Convert (520)<sub>10</sub> into base 16.
short.answer:
Divide repeatedly by 16:

  • 520 ÷ 16 = 32 remainder 8
  • 32 ÷ 16 = 2 remainder 0
  • 2 ÷ 16 = 0 remainder 2

Reading the remainders bottom to top: (208)16.

Check: 2×162 + 0×161 + 8×160 = 512 + 0 + 8 = 520. Correct.

short.question: What is number system?
short.answer:
A number system is a method of representing numbers using a set of digits or symbols, together with the rules that decide what a written number is worth.

The four used in computing are decimal (base 10), binary (base 2), octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16).

short.question: What is octal number system?
short.answer:
The octal number system is the base-8 system. It uses eight digits, 0 to 7 — there is no digit 8 or 9 — and every position is a power of 8.

It is written with a subscript 8, for example (237)8.

short.question: Convert (356)<sub>10</sub> into base 8.
short.answer:
Divide repeatedly by 8:

  • 356 ÷ 8 = 44 remainder 4
  • 44 ÷ 8 = 5 remainder 4
  • 5 ÷ 8 = 0 remainder 5

Reading the remainders bottom to top: (544)8.

Check: 5×82 + 4×81 + 4×80 = 320 + 32 + 4 = 356. Correct.

short.question: Convert 333 decimal numbers into Hexadecimal number and back to base two number systems.
short.answer:
Decimal to hexadecimal. Divide by 16:

  • 333 ÷ 16 = 20 remainder 13, which is written D
  • 20 ÷ 16 = 1 remainder 4
  • 1 ÷ 16 = 0 remainder 1

So 333 = (14D)16.

Hexadecimal to binary. Replace each hexadecimal digit with its four-bit binary group:

  • 1 → 0001
  • 4 → 0100
  • D (13) → 1101

Joined together: 0001 0100 1101, so 333 = (101001101)2.

Check: 256 + 64 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 333. Correct.

short.question: Convert (B8C)<sub>16</sub> hexadecimal number into base 10 number system.
short.answer:
First replace the letters with their values: B = 11, C = 12. So the digits are 11, 8, 12.

11×162 + 8×161 + 12×160

= 11×256 + 8×16 + 12×1

= 2816 + 128 + 12 = 2956

So (B8C)16 = (2956)10.

short.question: Convert decimal 14 to binary number system.
short.answer:
Divide repeatedly by 2:

  • 14 ÷ 2 = 7 remainder 0
  • 7 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 1
  • 3 ÷ 2 = 1 remainder 1
  • 1 ÷ 2 = 0 remainder 1

Reading the remainders bottom to top: (1110)2.

Check: 8 + 4 + 2 = 14. Correct.

long.question: What is number system? Explain the different number systems.
long.answer:
A number system is a method of representing numbers using a set of digits or symbols, along with the rules that determine what a written number is worth. Every system has a base (or radix) — the count of different digits it uses, and the value each position is multiplied by as you move left.

There are four systems used in computing:

1. Decimal (base 10). The system of everyday life. Ten digits, 0 to 9; each position is a power of 10. Written (345)10.

2. Binary (base 2). The system computers actually use. Two digits, 0 and 1; each position is a power of 2. Written (1001)2.

3. Octal (base 8). Eight digits, 0 to 7; each position is a power of 8. Written (237)8.

4. Hexadecimal (base 16). Sixteen symbols — the digits 0 to 9 and the letters A to F, standing for 10 to 15. Each position is a power of 16. Written (A26)16.

Why several? Binary is what the hardware does; but a long binary number is hard for a person to read, so octal and hexadecimal are used as a compact shorthand — one hexadecimal digit is exactly four binary digits.

long.question: What is decimal number system? How can you convert decimal number into octal number? Explain.
long.answer:
Decimal number system. The decimal system is the base-10 system used in daily life. It has ten digits, 0 to 9, and each position is a power of 10, so 345 means 3×102 + 4×101 + 5×100.

Converting decimal to octal. Divide the number by 8 repeatedly, keeping the remainder each time, until the quotient reaches 0. Then read the remainders from the bottom up.

  1. Divide the number by 8.
  2. Write the quotient underneath — it becomes the new number.
  3. Write the remainder to the right.
  4. Repeat until the quotient is 0.
  5. Read the remainders bottom to top; that is the octal number.

Example — (99)10 to octal:

  • 99 ÷ 8 = 12 remainder 3
  • 12 ÷ 8 = 1 remainder 4
  • 1 ÷ 8 = 0 remainder 1

Reading bottom to top: (143)8.

Check: 1×82 + 4×81 + 3×80 = 64 + 32 + 3 = 99. Correct.

long.question: Describe the process of converting a decimal number into binary and hexadecimal number systems with suitable examples.
long.answer:
Both use the same method — repeated division — and only the divisor changes: 2 for binary, 16 for hexadecimal.

The steps: divide by the new base; write the quotient underneath as the new number; note the remainder; repeat until the quotient is 0; then read the remainders from the bottom up.

Decimal to binary — (47)10:

  • 47 ÷ 2 = 23 r 1
  • 23 ÷ 2 = 11 r 1
  • 11 ÷ 2 = 5 r 1
  • 5 ÷ 2 = 2 r 1
  • 2 ÷ 2 = 1 r 0
  • 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1

Reading bottom to top: (101111)2.

Decimal to hexadecimal — (424)10:

  • 424 ÷ 16 = 26 r 8
  • 26 ÷ 16 = 1 r 10, written A
  • 1 ÷ 16 = 0 r 1

Reading bottom to top: (1A8)16.

The one thing to watch in hexadecimal: a remainder of 10 or more must be written as its letter — A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15.

Checking. Convert back: 1×162 + 10×161 + 8×160 = 256 + 160 + 8 = 424. Correct.

long.question: Describe the method of converting hexadecimal numbers into decimal numbers with an example.
long.answer:
To convert hexadecimal into decimal you multiply each digit by its place value and add. Place values rise as powers of 16 from the right, starting at 160.

  1. Number the positions from the right, starting at 0.
  2. Replace any letters with their values: A = 10, B = 11, C = 12, D = 13, E = 14, F = 15.
  3. Multiply each digit by 16 raised to its position number.
  4. Add the results.

Example — (1A8)16 to decimal. A is 10, so the digits are 1, 10 and 8:

1×162 + 10×161 + 8×160

= 1×256 + 10×16 + 8×1

= 256 + 160 + 8 = 424

So (1A8)16 = (424)10.

Second example — (B8C)16. B = 11 and C = 12, so:

11×256 + 8×16 + 12×1 = 2816 + 128 + 12 = 2956.

So (B8C)16 = (2956)10.

units.title: Data Communication and Computer Network
units.overview: How data travels between machines and how networks are built: the parts of a communication system, the modes and media it uses, network types and topologies, the devices that connect them, and the ideas behind the internet.
units.summary: Communication needs a sender, a message, a medium, a receiver and agreed rules. Networks are grouped by size from PAN to WAN, arranged in topologies, joined by devices such as hubs, switches and routers, and described by layered models. The internet is the network of all of them.

detailed.heading: Chapter 4 — Data Communication and Computer Network
detailed.note: Notes for Chapter 4 of the Class 8 book: how data travels, the media and networks it travels through, the devices that connect it, and the modern trends built on top.
learning_objectives: List the components of a data communication system
Compare simplex, half-duplex and full-duplex
Distinguish PAN, LAN, MAN and WAN and the common topologies
Describe the devices that join networks and the idea of a layered model

sections.title: Introduction to Data Communication and Computer Network

blocks.text: Every time you send a message, watch a video, join an online class or open a web page, information is travelling from one device to another. That movement is data communication.
The process of sending and receiving data — text, images, audio, video — between two or more devices through a medium such as a cable or a wireless signal.
A collection of two or more computers connected together, by cable or wireless signal, so that they can share information and resources.

When many devices are joined in this way, users can communicate, share files, use the internet and reach shared resources such as a printer. Those two ideas — communication and networks — are what make everyday digital life fast and convenient.
For data to get from one device to another, five things must be present. If any one is missing, communication fails.

items: Sender (source) — the device that produces and sends the data: a computer, a phone, a camera.
Message — the information itself: text, numbers, images, audio, video or a mixture.
Transmission medium — the physical or wireless path the data travels along.
Receiver (destination) — the device that takes the data in and turns the signal back into something usable.
Protocol — the set of rules both ends agree on so that what one sends, the other can understand.

blocks.text: Protocols are the part students most often skip, and they matter most. Without agreed rules, the receiver gets a stream of signals and no way to tell where one message ends and the next begins. Common examples:

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: A five-mark "components" answer needs all five, named and explained. The protocol is the one most often left out — always include it, and always give an example.
The communication mode is the direction data can flow between two devices. There are three, and the difference between them is the single most tested idea in this chapter.

head: Mode
Direction
Everyday example
rows: One way only — a device either sends or receives, never both
Radio or TV broadcast; a keyboard sending to the CPU
Both ways, but only one direction at a time
A walkie-talkie — you must wait for the other person to finish
Both ways at the same time
A telephone call; a mobile phone conversation

blocks.title: How to keep them straight
blocks.text: Simplex is a one-way street. Half-duplex is a narrow bridge — traffic both ways, one at a time. Full-duplex is a two-way highway — both directions at once.

Why is a walkie-talkie half-duplex and not full-duplex? Because only one person can talk at a time; if both spoke together neither would be understood. A telephone is full-duplex because both people can talk and be heard at once.

sections.title: Common Key Terms Used in Communication Media

blocks.text: Seven terms come up constantly when talking about how fast and how well a connection works. Several are easily confused.

How often a wave repeats itself in one second, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency carries more data but over a shorter distance; lower frequency travels further but carries less. A radio station at 100 MHz sends a signal that oscillates 100 million times a second.
A high-speed internet connection that is always on — far faster than the old dial-up. Home Wi-Fi, fibre, DSL and cable internet are all broadband.
The maximum amount of data that can travel through the connection at one time, measured in bits per second — Mbps or Gbps. A "100 Mbps plan" has a bandwidth of 100 Mbps.

The actual speed you get, which is nearly always less than the bandwidth because of congestion and other losses. If your plan promises 100 Mbps but you measure 60 Mbps, the bandwidth is 100 and the throughput is 60.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Bandwidth is what you are sold; throughput is what you get. Questions that mention "actual speed" or "speed experienced by the user" are asking about throughput, not bandwidth.

Launched

What it made possible

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The generations are asked about in two ways: which speed, and which applications. Learn the speed alongside the flagship use — 5G with remote surgery and smart cities, 4G with HD streaming and gaming, 3G with video calls and basic browsing.
The physical or wireless pathways along which data signals travel from a sender to a receiver.
There are two families: wired (guided) and wireless (unguided).
1. Wired transmission media (guided media)
Data travels along a physical cable on a fixed path.

head: Cable
What it does
Used for

Pairs of copper wire twisted together to cut interference

Very fast data over long distances

2. Wireless transmission media (unguided media)
Data travels through the air rather than along a cable.

head: Type
How it behaves
Used for

blocks.text: A computer network is two or more computers joined by cable or wireless signal so that they can share information and resources — files, printers, and communication.
Advantages of networking

items: Resource sharing — many users share one printer, scanner or set of files instead of copying them onto USB drives.
Easy communication — messages, email and video calls arrive instantly.
Internet access — every connected device can use the same connection.
Cost saving — one printer or one internet connection serves many computers.
Collaboration — a group can work on the same project from different places.
Data backup — important files can be kept on another machine or a server for safety.

head: Type
Full form
Covers
Example
rows: A Bluetooth headset linked to a phone
One building or site — home, school, office
Branches of a bank across one city

blocks.text: PAN (Personal Area Network)
A PAN links personal devices over a very short range, typically around 10 metres — a phone, laptop, tablet, wireless earbuds or a smartwatch.

items: Range: up to 10 metres
Purpose: personal use, linking your own devices
Examples: phone to Bluetooth headset; laptop to phone by hotspot; smartwatch to phone

blocks.text: Advantages: quick and simple to set up with technologies such as Bluetooth; highly portable; low power consumption, so it does not drain the battery.
LAN (Local Area Network)

A LAN covers a small area such as a home, a school or one group of buildings. It offers high data-transmission speed over a short distance, is simple to run, and uses cheap devices such as hubs, switches and network cards.
MAN (Metropolitan Area Network)
A MAN spans a city or town — larger than a LAN, smaller than a WAN. It is typically used to link the branches of one organisation across a city.
WAN (Wide Area Network)
A WAN covers a large geographical area — cities, countries or continents — and the internet is the largest example.

Disadvantages: the equipment is more expensive than for a LAN or MAN; transmission is slower; it is complex to build, manage and secure; and it needs skilled staff and often the involvement of government agencies.
