teaching_plan.activity: Ask why a video holds attention better than a paragraph. Define multimedia and list the five application areas, then weigh the three advantages against the three disadvantages.
Take one short video and pause it, asking pupils to name every component they can see or hear. Then draw out the video-versus-animation distinction: recorded versus constructed.
Save the same picture as JPG and PNG and compare the file sizes. Show a logo on a coloured background in both, so the transparency difference is obvious.
Play the same track as WAV and MP3, compare sizes, and ask what was traded away. Contrast compressed with uncompressed formats.
Show the same clip at low and high frame rate (smoothness) and at low and high resolution (detail), so the two ideas are kept apart. Then cover MP4, AVI and MOV.
Show a 2D cartoon and a 3D film clip side by side and build the comparison table from what pupils notice. Walk through the six steps of the animation process.
Work through the Audacity tasks in a computer lab, then the CapCut tasks. Set the exercise questions as homework.

units.title: Contemporary Technologies
units.overview: The technologies shaping computing now: artificial intelligence and generative AI, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, digital communication, virtual and augmented reality, and online commerce.
units.summary: AI lets machines do tasks that used to need people, generative AI produces new content, IoT connects everyday objects, cloud computing moves storage and processing off your machine, VR and AR change what you see, and e-commerce moves buying and paying online.

detailed.heading: Chapter 9 — Contemporary Technologies
detailed.note: Notes for Chapter 9 of the Class 8 book: modern technology, artificial intelligence and generative AI, the Internet of Things, cloud computing, digital communication, virtual and augmented reality, and e-commerce.
learning_objectives: Describe artificial intelligence and generative AI
Explain the Internet of Things and cloud computing
Describe VR, AR and how e-commerce works

blocks.text: Technology is changing the way we live, learn and communicate every day. From mobile phones and the internet to online classes and digital payments, modern life is closely tied to it. In earlier times people depended on simple tools and manual work; today technology helps us finish tasks faster, more easily and more accurately.

This chapter looks at the technologies we actually meet in daily life: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Generative AI, the Internet of Things (IoT), cloud computing, digital communication tools, Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR), and e-commerce.

You attend an online class on a phone. Your parents withdraw money from an ATM. A teacher explains a lesson with a video. A message reaches a friend in seconds. All of these are modern technology at work.
Using knowledge, tools, machines and methods to solve problems and make life easier. People have used technology since ancient times — stone for cutting, fire for cooking, simple tools for farming.
Advanced technology that is fast, digital, and usually connected through the internet. It helps us work faster and more efficiently than the manual tools of the past.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Technology and modern technology are not the same thing. A stone axe is technology. A smartphone is modern technology — digital, fast and connected.
Past and present compared
The pattern is the same every time: what once needed time and effort is now digital and automatic. A letter took several days; a message is instant.
Examples from daily life

items: Smartphones — communication, learning, entertainment and information, all in one device.
The internet — connects people and devices across the world.
ATM (Automated Teller Machine) — withdraw money, check balances and do other banking tasks without queuing at a counter.
Smart classrooms — projectors, computers and smart boards, with videos and presentations to explain lessons clearly.

blocks.text: Importance in daily life

head: Area
How modern technology helps
rows: Learning through videos, animations and online resources; online classes and digital libraries
Instant contact by call, message and video chat
Computers and software get tasks done efficiently
Machines for diagnosis and treatment; cameras and alarms
Paying bills online, booking tickets, ordering food

blocks.title: A real example
blocks.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic many schools in Nepal ran classes through Zoom and Google Classroom, and students kept studying from home on their phones. That is modern technology supporting society in a difficult time.

You speak to your phone and it answers. Your phone unlocks by recognising your face. YouTube suggests videos like the ones you watched before. No human is doing these things directly — they happen because of Artificial Intelligence.
The technology that allows computers and machines to perform tasks that normally need human thinking and decision-making. In simple terms, it helps machines behave in a smart way.
An AI system can recognise images and voices, understand spoken words, learn from data, and make decisions.

blocks.title: Important
blocks.text: AI does not think the way a human does. It works from the programs and data people give it. It can be wrong, and it has no understanding of what it is doing.
Examples of AI in daily life

items: Voice assistants — Google Assistant, Siri and Alexa understand voice commands and reply. Ask "What is the weather today?" and you get an answer.
Face unlock — the phone recognises your face, so you do not need to type a password.
Video recommendations — YouTube and TikTok suggest videos from what you have watched; watch science videos and more science appears.
Language support — translation tools, useful when you want an English word explained in Nepali.
Navigation apps — Google Maps uses AI to pick the fastest route.
Shopping apps — suggestions based on what you searched for before.
Email spam filtering — unwanted mail is moved to the spam folder automatically.

blocks.text: Advantages of AI

head: Advantage
What it means
rows: Tasks such as finding information or getting directions finish quickly
Help with navigation, translation and reminders
Students use AI tools to understand lessons and explore topics
Fewer errors in calculations and data processing
AI tools are there at any hour

blocks.text: Ask a question online and a full explanation appears in seconds. A tool writes a paragraph for you. A system draws a picture from your description. That is Generative AI.
A type of Artificial Intelligence that creates new content — text, images or answers — from what the user asks. It produces new information rather than only showing stored data.

blocks.title: The difference from ordinary AI
blocks.text: Basic AI suggests or recognises — it picks a video, unlocks your phone. Generative AI produces — it writes sentences and paragraphs, answers in detail, and creates images and ideas.
Examples of Generative AI tools

head: Tool
What it does
Example
rows: Answers questions, explains topics, helps write content
Ask "Explain photosynthesis" and get a simple explanation
Explanations, summaries and ideas for learning
Describe "a mountain with snow and a river" and it draws one
Creates and edits short videos with AI
A simple animated video for a school project

blocks.text: Uses

items: Asking questions about any subject and getting a quick response.
Writing short paragraphs — paragraphs, stories, summaries.
Creating images for projects and assignments.
Creating videos or presentations.
Idea generation — projects, essays, creative work.

blocks.text: Responsible use

items: Use it for learning — to understand a topic, not just to finish the homework.
Check the information — AI sometimes gives wrong answers. Verify with books or your teacher.
Avoid misuse — do not copy answers straight into an exam or assignment.
Think independently — learn to write and think for yourself.

blocks.title: What responsible use looks like
blocks.text: A student uses a tool to understand a science lesson, then rewrites the explanation in their own words and discusses it with the teacher. Using it to understand is learning; handing in its words as yours is not.

A television connects to Wi-Fi and plays videos. A smartwatch counts your steps and shows your heart rate. A security camera at home can be checked from your phone. None of these devices is working alone — they are connected through the internet.
A system where everyday devices are connected to the Internet so they can share information and work automatically. IoT connects smart devices to make life easier.
An electronic device that connects to the Internet and performs tasks automatically — a smart TV or a smartwatch, for example.
Examples and uses of IoT devices

head: Device
Area
Use
rows: Connects to the internet for videos, browsing and apps — a student watches an educational video at home
Track steps, heart rate, sleep and calories burned
Smart lights, cameras and speakers controlled from a phone
Locks and unlocks the door under remote control

blocks.text: You take photos on your phone and later see them on another device. Your teacher shares notes online and you open them at home. You send files to a friend without a pen drive. All of that is cloud computing.

Storing data and using services through the Internet instead of keeping everything on your own device. Files are saved online and are not tied to one device — you can reach them any time you have the Internet.
Examples

items: Google Drive — stores documents, photos and videos online.
Online photo storage — phones often back photos up automatically, so they survive the loss of the handset.
Online document editing (Google Docs) — create and edit documents without installing software.
Email services — mail and attachments live online and can be opened any time.

blocks.text: Advantages

head: Advantage
What it means
rows: Open files from any place using the internet
Share without pen drives or other physical storage
Data survives even if the device is damaged or lost
Files live online, so the device stays free
Several people work on the same file together
Files are saved without you doing anything

blocks.title: A practical example
blocks.text: Teachers upload notes and assignments to an online platform; students open them at home and submit their work the same way. That is cloud computing supporting learning.
The process of sending and receiving information using electronic devices and the Internet.
These tools let people share messages, files, images and videos. They make communication easier, save time, support distance learning, and get information where it is needed quickly.

blocks.title: A practical example
blocks.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic many schools in Nepal taught through Zoom and Google Classroom. Students attended from home and submitted work digitally — digital communication keeping education running.
Types of digital communication

items: Email — electronic mail, used to send messages and files over the internet.
Messaging — apps giving instant communication by text, voice and video, such as classmates arranging group study.
Online classes and meetings — video conferencing lets students and teachers meet and interact in real time.

blocks.text: Importance in education

head: Point
What it means
rows: Students attend classes from any location
Teachers and students reach each other quickly
Notes, videos and assignments pass around easily
Students work together in discussions and group activities

blocks.text: You put on special goggles and feel as though you are somewhere else entirely. Or you point your phone at a table and a 3D model of a planet appears on it. The first is VR, the second is AR.
A technology that creates a completely computer-generated environment, taking the user into a fully virtual world. It usually needs a special headset giving 3D visuals and sound.
A technology that adds digital objects to the real-world environment — it puts digital elements into what you can already see. It runs on a phone or tablet and needs no special headset.
Differences between VR and AR

head: Basis
Virtual Reality (VR)
Augmented Reality (AR)
rows: The real world, with digital objects added
Phone or tablet — no headset needed
Exploring space, oceans or historical sites
A 3D model of an animal or planet on your desk

blocks.text: Examples and uses in daily life

head: Area
How VR and AR are used
rows: Interactive experiences; some games let you move physically and handle virtual objects
VR takes students into virtual science labs; AR shows 3D diagrams for science and geography
VR lets you visit museums and landmarks without travelling
AR shows how a piece of furniture would look in your room
VR gives pilots and doctors a safe place to practise

blocks.title: A practical example
blocks.text: Some schools and learning centres in Nepal use digital simulations and 3D models to teach topics such as the solar system. Students understand better when they can see and turn the model rather than only read about it.
Your family orders clothes or books on a phone. The electricity or internet bill is paid online. A customer pays a shop by scanning a QR code. These are e-commerce and digital transactions.
Buying and selling goods or services through the Internet. People can search for products, compare prices, place orders and pay — all without visiting a shop.
Paying money electronically — by mobile phone, card or online system — instead of with cash.
Examples of digital payment

head: Method
Used for
rows: Bill payments, mobile recharge, money transfer
Online payments, ticket booking and transfers
Transferring money, paying bills, checking balances
Paying instantly by scanning a code
ATM, debit and credit cards for payment and cash withdrawal

blocks.text: Benefits

head: Benefit
What it means
rows: Shop or pay bills without travelling
Receipts and transaction history for reference
Little or no physical cash to carry

blocks.text: Precautions

items: Keep passwords safe — never share a PIN or password with anyone.
Use trusted apps only — download payment apps from the official app stores.
Check before paying — confirm the amount and the receiver before you send money.
Avoid unknown links — do not click suspicious payment links.
Log out after use — always, on shared or public devices.
Keep devices secure — use a screen lock and keep apps up to date.

blocks.title: A practical example
blocks.text: Many shops in Nepal now use QR code payment. The customer scans the code in eSewa, Khalti or a bank app and pays at once — fast for both sides. But it is still worth checking the amount and the receiver before you confirm.

short.question: What is modern technology? Give one example.
short.answer:
Modern technology is advanced technology that is fast, digital, and usually connected through the internet. It helps us work faster and more efficiently than the manual tools of the past.

Example: the smartphone, which handles communication, learning, entertainment and information all at once.

short.question: Define Artificial Intelligence. Write one daily-life example.
short.answer:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the technology that lets computers and machines do tasks that normally need human thinking and decision-making — recognising images and voices, understanding speech, learning from data and making decisions.

It is worth remembering that AI does not think as a human does; it works from the programs and data it was given.

Example: face unlock on a phone, which recognises your face so you do not have to type a password.

short.question: What is Generative AI? Write one use for students.
short.answer:
Generative AI is a type of AI that creates new content — text, images or answers — from what the user asks. It produces new information rather than only showing stored data.

Use for students: asking for an explanation of a difficult topic, then rewriting it in their own words. It can also help draft paragraphs, create images for a project, or suggest ideas.

short.question: What is IoT? Give one example from daily life.
short.answer:
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system where everyday devices are connected to the Internet so they can share information and work automatically.

Example: a smart TV that connects to Wi-Fi and plays videos, or a smartwatch that counts your steps and tracks your heart rate.

short.question: What is cloud computing? Write one advantage.
short.answer:
Cloud computing means storing data and using services through the Internet instead of keeping everything on your own device. Your files live online, so they are not tied to one machine.

Advantage: you can reach your files from anywhere. (Others: easy sharing, safe storage if the device is lost, saves space on the device, several people can work on one file, automatic backup.)

short.question: Name any two digital communication tools used in education.
short.answer:
1. Email — for sending messages and files, such as homework handed to a teacher.
  2. Messaging apps — instant text, voice and video, which is how many classes arrange group study.

Also acceptable: online class and meeting platforms such as Zoom or Google Classroom, where students and teachers meet in real time.

short.question: Differentiate between VR and AR (one point).
short.answer:
Virtual Reality creates a completely computer-generated environment and takes you into a fully virtual world, usually through a headset. Augmented Reality adds digital objects to the real world around you — you stay where you are, and it works on a phone or tablet with no headset.

In short: VR replaces the world you see; AR adds to it.

short.question: What is digital payment? Give one example.
short.answer:
A digital payment is paying money electronically — by mobile phone, card or online system — instead of with cash.

Example: scanning a QR code with eSewa, Khalti or a bank app and paying at once. Others include mobile banking apps and debit or credit cards.

long.question: Explain modern technology with examples from daily life.
long.answer:
Technology means using knowledge, tools, machines and methods to solve problems and make life easier; people have done it since ancient times, with stone tools, fire and simple farm implements. Modern technology is the advanced form: fast, digital, and usually connected through the internet. It helps us work faster and more efficiently.

Examples from daily life:

  • Smartphones — communication, learning, entertainment and information in one device.
  • The internet — connecting people and devices across the world.
  • ATMs — withdrawing money and checking balances without queuing at a counter.
  • Smart classrooms — projectors, computers and smart boards so teachers can explain with video and presentations.

Past and present. Each of these replaced something slower: letters became email and messaging, manual tools became tractors, the chalkboard became the smartboard, cash became digital payment, and film cameras became digital ones.

Importance. Modern technology matters in education (videos, animations, online classes and digital libraries), communication (instant calls, messages and video chat), work and business (computers and software), health and safety (diagnostic machines, cameras and alarms), and everyday convenience (paying bills, booking tickets, ordering food). During the COVID-19 pandemic schools in Nepal kept teaching through Zoom and Google Classroom — modern technology holding society together.

long.question: Describe Artificial Intelligence and its benefits in daily life.
long.answer:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is the technology that lets computers and machines do tasks that normally require human thinking and decision-making. An AI system can recognise images and voices, understand spoken words, learn from data and make decisions. In simple terms, it helps machines behave in a smart way.

It should be said plainly, though: AI does not think the way a human does. It works from the programs and data people have given it.

Examples in daily life: voice assistants such as Google Assistant, Siri and Alexa; face unlock on a phone; video recommendations on YouTube and TikTok; translation tools; navigation apps choosing the fastest route; shopping apps suggesting products; and spam filtering that clears junk mail for you.

Benefits:

BenefitWhat it means
Saves timeFinding information or getting directions is quick
Makes life easierHelp with navigation, translation and reminders
Supports learningStudents use AI tools to understand lessons and explore topics
Improves accuracyFewer errors in calculation and data processing
Personalized experienceSuggestions match your interests
24/7 availabilityThe tools are there at any hour
Helps in safety and securityFace recognition and surveillance cameras

long.question: Explain Generative AI and write its responsible uses for students.
long.answer:
Generative AI is a type of AI that creates new content — text, images or answers — based on what the user asks. It produces new information rather than only showing stored data.

That is what separates it from ordinary AI: basic AI suggests or recognises (picking a video, unlocking a phone), while generative AI produces — writing sentences and paragraphs, answering in detail, and creating images and ideas.

Tools: ChatGPT answers questions and explains topics; Gemini gives explanations and summaries; DALL-E draws images from a description; Runway ML creates and edits short videos.

Uses: asking questions, writing short paragraphs and summaries, creating images for projects, creating videos or presentations, and generating ideas.

Responsible use:

  1. Use it for learning — to understand a topic, not just to get the homework finished.
  2. Check the information — it sometimes gives wrong answers, so verify against your books or your teacher.
  3. Avoid misuse — do not copy its answers straight into an exam or an assignment.
  4. Think independently — learn to write and reason for yourself.

The right pattern is to read its explanation, close it, and rewrite the point in your own words — the way you would with any reference book. Then discuss it with your teacher. Understanding is learning; handing in its words as yours is not.

long.question: What is IoT? Explain its uses in daily life with examples.
long.answer:
The Internet of Things (IoT) is a system where everyday devices are connected to the Internet so that they can share information and work automatically. It connects smart devices to make life easier. A smart device is an electronic device that connects to the internet and performs tasks by itself — a smart TV or a smartwatch, for instance.

The point is that these devices are not working alone. A television that streams video over Wi-Fi, a watch that counts your steps, and a security camera you can check from your phone are all part of the same idea.

Uses in daily life:

DeviceAreaUse
Smart TVHome and educationVideo, browsing and apps — a student watches an educational video at home
Smartwatch, fitness bandsHealthSteps, heart rate, sleep, calories
Smart home devicesHome and securityLights, cameras and speakers controlled from a phone
Smart door lockSecurityLocking and unlocking remotely
Navigation systemsTransportGuidance and routing
Smart energy devicesEnergyCutting wasted power
Smart farming devicesAgricultureMonitoring crops and soil

long.question: Explain cloud computing with examples and advantages.
long.answer:
Cloud computing means storing data and using services through the Internet instead of keeping everything on your own device. You save and reach your files online, so they are not tied to one machine — you can get at them any time you have a connection.

It is what lets you photograph something on your phone and see it later on a laptop, or send a file to a friend without hunting for a pen drive.

Examples: Google Drive, which stores documents, photos and videos; online photo storage, which backs your pictures up automatically so they survive the loss of the handset; Google Docs, which lets you write and edit without installing anything; and email, whose messages and attachments live online.

Advantages:

AdvantageWhat it means
Access anywhereOpen your files from any place
Easy sharingNo pen drives or other physical storage needed
Safe storageData survives damage or loss of the device
Saves storage spaceThe device itself stays free
Supports collaborationSeveral people work on the same file
Automatic backupFiles are saved without your having to remember

In schools this is now ordinary: a teacher uploads the notes, students open them at home and hand their work back the same way.

long.question: Describe digital communication tools and their importance in education.
long.answer:
Digital communication is the sending and receiving of information using electronic devices and the Internet. These tools let people share messages, files, images and videos; they make communication easier, save time, support distance learning, and get information where it is needed quickly.

Types:

  1. Email — electronic mail, for messages and files over the internet.
  2. Messaging — apps giving instant contact by text, voice and video, the way classmates arrange group study.
  3. Online classes and meetings — video conferencing, where students and teachers meet and interact in real time.

Importance in education:

PointWhat it means
Learning from anywhereStudents attend classes from any location
Fast communicationTeachers and students reach each other quickly
Easy sharing of materialsNotes, videos and assignments pass around easily
Supports group learningStudents work together in discussions and group work

The clearest evidence came during the COVID-19 pandemic, when many schools in Nepal taught through Zoom and Google Classroom and students submitted their work from home.

long.question: Explain Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality with examples.
long.answer:
Virtual Reality (VR) creates a completely computer-generated environment, taking the user into a fully virtual world. It usually needs a special headset supplying 3D visuals and sound. Augmented Reality (AR) adds digital objects to the real-world environment — it puts digital elements into what you can already see. It runs on a phone or tablet and needs no special headset.

The difference in one line: VR replaces the world you see; AR adds to it.

BasisVRAR
The worldCompletely computer-generatedThe real world with digital objects added
EquipmentSpecial headsetPhone or tablet
Where you areInside a virtual worldWhere you already are

Uses:

  • Games and entertainment — interactive play where you move and handle virtual objects.
  • Education — VR takes students into a virtual science lab; AR shows 3D diagrams for science and geography.
  • Virtual tours — visiting museums and landmarks without travelling.
  • Shopping and design — AR shows how a piece of furniture would look in your room.
  • Training — VR gives pilots and doctors a safe place to practise.

Some schools and learning centres in Nepal already use digital simulations and 3D models for topics such as the solar system; pupils understand better when they can turn the model rather than only read about it.

long.question: What is e-commerce? Explain its benefits and precautions.
long.answer:
E-commerce (electronic commerce) is buying and selling goods or services through the Internet. People search for products, compare prices, place orders and pay — without going to a shop.

A digital transaction is paying money electronically — by mobile phone, card or online system — instead of with cash.

Examples of digital payment in Nepal: eSewa for bills, recharge and transfers; Khalti for online payment, tickets and transfers; mobile banking apps for transfers, bills and balances; QR code payments made by scanning; and ATM, debit and credit cards.

Benefits:

BenefitWhat it means
Saves timeShop or pay bills without travelling
ConvenientPay any time, anywhere
Easy comparisonCompare prices before buying
Provides recordsReceipts and history to refer back to
Reduces cash handlingLittle or no physical cash to carry
Faster transactionsPayments complete instantly
Supports online servicesTickets, school fees, food orders

Precautions:

  1. Keep passwords safe — never share a PIN or password.
  2. Use trusted apps only — install payment apps from the official stores.
  3. Check before paying — confirm the amount and the receiver.
  4. Avoid unknown links — do not click suspicious payment links.
  5. Log out after use — always, on shared or public devices.
  6. Keep devices secure — screen lock, and keep apps up to date.

QR payment is now common in shops across Nepal: scan the code in eSewa, Khalti or a bank app and pay on the spot. Fast for everyone — but still check the amount and the receiver before you confirm.

teaching_plan.activity: Ask pupils to list every piece of technology they touched before school. Define technology and modern technology, then build the past-versus-present table from their examples.

units.title: Computer Ethics, Data Privacy and Cyber Security
units.overview: Behaving properly and staying safe online: what computer ethics covers, what data privacy means and why it matters, and the practical steps that make up cyber security.
units.summary: Ethics covers how you ought to behave with other people's work and data, privacy covers what may be collected about you and how it must be looked after, and security covers the measures that keep it out of the wrong hands.

detailed.heading: Chapter 10 — Computer Ethics, Data Privacy and Cyber Security
detailed.chapter_title: Computer Ethics, Data Privacy and Cyber Security
detailed.note: Notes for Chapter 10 of the Class 8 book: computer ethics, data privacy and how to protect it, and cyber security — its types, the threats it answers, and why it matters.
learning_objectives: Explain what computer ethics covers
Describe what data privacy means and why it matters
List practical cyber security measures

blocks.text: Computers raise questions that hardware alone cannot answer. May you open a file that belongs to someone else? May you copy software you did not pay for? May you post something about a classmate that you would never say to their face? Computer ethics is the part of the subject that answers those questions.

The moral principles and guidelines that govern the use of computers and information technology. It is about what is right and wrong when using computers, networks and digital information — including digital privacy and security, intellectual property, acceptable online behaviour, and the responsible use of technology.
Advantages of computer ethics

head: Advantage
What it means
rows: Personal data is kept safe and confidential
Ethical behaviour means less hacking, fraud and misuse
Users learn how to use technology properly
Organisations can follow laws and regulations
Discourages piracy and illegal copying of software and content

blocks.text: Key areas of computer ethics

items: Privacy. Protecting personal information held in computer systems, and respecting other people's confidentiality. You have the right to control how your own data is collected, used and shared. Example: an employee not passing customer credit card numbers or home addresses to anyone unauthorised.

Intellectual property rights. Respecting ownership of digital content — software, music, creative work — which protects the people who made it and discourages illegal copying. Example: buying a software licence rather than downloading a cracked version.

Preventing harm and cybercrime. Using technology for productive, ethical purposes and not to damage other people's data or systems. Following these guidelines reduces hacking, data theft, identity theft and piracy. Example: not writing, spreading or installing malware or phishing software.
Respectful online behaviour. Treating others with respect online and avoiding harassment. Example: refraining from cyberbullying or spreading malicious rumours on social media.

Security. Protecting systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, damage or theft — using strong passwords, antivirus software and firewalls, and never taking access you were not given. Example: not trying to break into someone else's email or a company database, even when it is poorly protected.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: The last point is the one students most often miss: walking away from an open door is part of ethics, not just part of security. That a system is easy to break into does not make breaking into it acceptable.

head: Importance

Limits how much personal information is collected and shared; systems verify identity with a password, an OTP or a biometric

blocks.text: Methods to protect data privacy

items: Use strong passwords. Length matters most: aim for 12–16 characters, mixing uppercase (A–Z), lowercase (a–z), numbers (0–9) and special characters (@, $, %).

Enable two-factor authentication (2FA). This adds a second kind of check. Normally you log in with something you know — your password. With 2FA you also need something you have (your phone, an app) or something you are (a fingerprint or face scan). A six-digit code sent by text message is the common form.
Avoid sharing sensitive information online.
Follow data protection laws.

blocks.title: What counts as sensitive
blocks.text: Anything that could identify you or open your accounts: passwords and PINs, bank and card details, OTPs, citizenship or ID numbers, home address and phone number, personal photos and private messages, and the answers to your security questions.

blocks.title: Following data protection law
blocks.text: Collect data only for valid, legal purposes; use it only for the purpose it was collected for; and protect it with encryption, passwords and firewalls.
The practice of protecting computers, networks, systems and data from digital attacks, unauthorised access and damage.

head: Importance
What it means
rows: Safeguards personal, financial and business information; prevents unauthorised access and leaks
Covers hacking, phishing, malware and ransomware, and so reduces damage and theft
Keeps user information confidential and stops misuse of personal data
Prevents failures and downtime, so organisations keep running
Avoids losses from cyber fraud and theft, and the cost of recovering from a breach

blocks.text: How to set a strong password
Three things matter: length, complexity and uniqueness. Experts now recommend a minimum of 12 to 16 characters.

items: Characters — mix uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols such as !, @, # and $.
Avoid sequences — not "12345", not "abcd", not keyboard patterns like "qwerty".
No personal information — not your name, birth date, pet's name or address, since these are easily found on social media.

blocks.title: Exam note
blocks.text: Of the three, length is the most important. A longer password beats a short complicated one. And a strong password used on every site is not strong at all — one breach exposes all your accounts, which is why uniqueness matters.

short.question: What is computer ethics?
short.answer:
Computer ethics is the set of moral principles and guidelines that govern the use of computers and information technology. It is about what is right and wrong when using computers, networks and digital information — covering digital privacy and security, intellectual property, acceptable online behaviour, and the responsible use of technology.

Its five key areas are privacy, intellectual property rights, preventing harm and cybercrime, respectful online behaviour, and security.

short.question: What is intellectual property rights?
short.answer:
Intellectual property rights are the ownership rights over software, data, digital content and other creations of the mind. Respecting them means acknowledging that the person who made something owns it.

They protect software developers, authors and creators by discouraging illegal copying and distribution.

Example: buying a software licence instead of downloading a pirated or cracked version.

short.question: Define data privacy.
short.answer:
Data privacy is the protection of personal and sensitive information from unauthorised access, use or disclosure. It ensures that each person has control over how their data is collected, stored and shared.

It covers personal data (name, address, phone, email), sensitive data (passwords, bank details, health records), behavioural data (browsing and search history, app usage) and biometric data (fingerprints, facial recognition).

short.question: What is personal data?
short.answer:
Personal data is the information that identifies you as an individual — your name, address, phone number and email address.

It is the first of four types the chapter names. The others are sensitive data (passwords, bank details, health records), behavioural data (browsing history, search activity, app usage) and biometric data (fingerprints, facial recognition). Personal data alone usually identifies you; the others are what you then need to protect most carefully.

short.question: What is cyber security?
short.answer:
Cyber security is the practice of protecting computers, networks, systems and data from digital attacks, unauthorised access and damage.

Its five types are network security, information security, application security, cloud security and endpoint security.

short.question: Define malware.
short.answer:
Malware (malicious software) is software written to harm a computer, a network or its user. The term covers viruses, which attach themselves to other programs and spread; worms, which spread on their own across networks; and ransomware, which locks your data and demands payment to release it.

Alongside phishing and hacking, it is one of the common threats cyber security exists to stop.

long.question: Explain the advantages of computer ethics.
long.answer:
Computer ethics is the set of moral principles and guidelines that govern the use of computers and information technology — what is right and wrong when using computers, networks and digital information.

Following it has five advantages:

AdvantageWhat it means
Protects privacyPersonal data is kept safe and confidential
Reduces cybercrimeEthical behaviour means less hacking, fraud and misuse
Promotes responsible useUsers understand how to use technology properly
Supports legal complianceOrganisations can follow laws and regulations
Encourages fair use of resourcesDiscourages piracy and illegal copying of software and content

The thread connecting them is that ethics prevents harm before any technical safeguard is needed. A firewall can stop an attacker; only a sense of what is right stops someone from becoming one.

long.question: Explain key areas of computer ethics.
long.answer:
Computer ethics covers five areas.

1. Privacy. Protecting personal information held in computer systems, and respecting other people's confidentiality. Individuals have the right to control how their data is collected, used and shared. Example: an employee not sharing customer credit card numbers or home addresses with anyone unauthorised.

2. Intellectual property rights. Respecting ownership of digital content — software, music and creative work — which protects developers, authors and creators and discourages illegal copying. Example: buying a licence rather than downloading a cracked version.

3. Preventing harm and cybercrime. Using technology productively rather than to damage other people's data or systems. Following these guidelines reduces hacking, data theft, identity theft and piracy. Example: not writing, spreading or installing malware or phishing software.

4. Respectful online behaviour. Treating others with respect online and avoiding harassment. Example: refraining from cyberbullying or spreading malicious rumours on social media.

5. Security. Protecting systems, networks and data from unauthorised access, damage or theft, using strong passwords, antivirus software and firewalls — and never taking access you were not given. Example: not trying to break into someone else's email or a company database, even if it is poorly protected.

That last point is worth dwelling on. Walking away from an open door is an ethical act, not merely a secure one — that a system is easy to break into does not make breaking into it acceptable.

long.question: What are the types of data involved in privacy? Explain.
long.answer:
Data privacy is the protection of personal and sensitive information from unauthorised access, use or disclosure. Four types of data are involved.

TypeWhat it includesWhy it needs protecting
Personal dataName, address, phone number, emailIt identifies you, and can be used to impersonate you
Sensitive dataPasswords, bank details, health recordsAnyone holding it can reach your accounts and your money
Behavioural dataBrowsing history, search activity, app usageIt builds a detailed picture of you without your noticing
Biometric dataFingerprints, facial recognitionUnlike a password, you cannot change your fingerprints if they are stolen

The four call for different care. Personal data is often public and only mildly risky; sensitive data is the kind criminals want; behavioural data is collected quietly and in volume; and biometric data is the hardest to recover from, because it cannot be reissued.

long.question: Explain the importance of data privacy.
long.answer:
Data privacy means individuals keep control over how their data is collected, stored and shared. It matters for five reasons.

ImportanceWhat it means
Protects personal informationPasswords, bank details and identity information stay safe; data is encrypted, only you can log in, and nothing is shared without permission
Prevents identity theft and fraudRules limit how much personal information is collected and shared, and systems verify identity with a password, an OTP or a biometric
Maintains confidentialityPrivate information is seen only by authorised people — essential in business, healthcare and government
Prevents data misuseStops data being used for purposes you never agreed to, and protects users from manipulation
Enhances securityEncourages encryption, firewalls and secure systems, so breaches become less likely

Put simply: privacy is what turns a collection of facts about you into information you control rather than information someone else holds.

long.question: Explain the types of cyber security.
long.answer:
Cyber security is the practice of protecting computers, networks, systems and data from digital attacks, unauthorised access and damage. It has five types.

TypeWhat it protects
Network securityComputer networks, from intrusions and attacks
Information securityData, from unauthorised access or modification
Application securitySoftware and applications, from vulnerabilities
Cloud securityData stored in cloud systems
Endpoint securityThe devices themselves — computers, smartphones and tablets

The five are best understood as layers. Network security guards the road, information security guards the contents, application security guards the programs that handle them, cloud security guards the copies kept elsewhere, and endpoint security guards the device in your hand. A weakness in any one of them undoes the work of the others.

The threats they face are malware, phishing, hacking and ransomware, and the measures that answer them are strong passwords, two-factor authentication, avoiding suspicious links and emails, antivirus software, and secured networks.

long.question: Explain the importance of cyber security.
long.answer:
Cyber security is the practice of protecting computers, networks, systems and data from digital attacks, unauthorised access and damage. It is a vital part of Information Technology, and it matters for five reasons.

ImportanceWhat it means
Protects sensitive dataSafeguards personal, financial and business information, and prevents unauthorised access and data leaks
Prevents cyber attacksDefends against hacking, phishing, malware and ransomware, reducing damage and theft
Ensures privacyKeeps user information confidential and prevents misuse of personal data
Maintains business continuityPrevents failures and downtime, so organisations keep operating
Prevents financial lossAvoids the losses caused by cyber fraud and theft, and the cost of recovering after a breach

Notice that the last two are about consequences that spread. A successful attack does not stop with the person attacked — it can close a school office, empty a company account, or put a hospital's records out of reach.

mcq.question: Computer ethics deals with:
mcq.teacher_note: Ethics is about right and wrong. Hardware, networking and programming are technical subjects, not moral ones.

mcq.question: Unauthorized copying of software is called:
mcq.teacher_note: Copying software you have no licence for is piracy. Hacking is unauthorised access, phishing is stealing information with fake messages, and spamming is sending unwanted bulk mail.

mcq.question: Which is an example of unethical behavior?
mcq.teacher_note: Of the four, only breaking into a system harms someone. The other three are all good practice.

mcq.question: Intellectual property refers to:
mcq.teacher_note: Intellectual property is something you created with your mind — a piece of software, a song, a book. Physical goods and hardware are not intellectual property.

mcq.question: Ethical use of computers includes:
mcq.teacher_note: Three of these are crimes. Respecting other people's privacy is the ethical behaviour.

mcq.question: Spreading false information online is:
mcq.teacher_note: Deliberately spreading something untrue to mislead people is unethical. It is not made acceptable by being common.

mcq.question: Data privacy means:
mcq.teacher_note: Privacy is about protection and control over who sees your data. Deleting and storing say nothing about who is allowed to look.

mcq.question: Strong password should include:
mcq.teacher_note: A strong password mixes uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols. Any password built from only one kind of character is weak.

mcq.question: Two-factor authentication improves:
mcq.teacher_note: 2FA adds a second check before you can log in — it is slower, not faster, but far harder to break.

mcq.question: Cyber security protects:
mcq.teacher_note: The clue is in the word: cyber. It protects computers, networks and data, not physical objects.

teaching_plan.topic: Data privacy and the four types of data
teaching_plan.activity: Define data privacy, then take each of the four types and ask what harm would follow if it leaked. Pupils usually notice that biometric data cannot be reissued — build on that.
Cover the five principles and the five reasons privacy matters, then move to the practical methods. Demonstrate enabling 2FA on a spare account.
